newsitem.title: USA: Dole plea to Perot could lead to even worse loss.
newsitem.headline: Dole plea to Perot could lead to even worse loss.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Bob Dole's plea to Texas billionaire Ross Perot to quit the presidential race smacks of desperation and could further weaken the Republican nominee's support, political analysts said on Thursday.

Dole, trailing President Bill Clinton in polls by between nine and 16 percentage points 12 days before Election Day, sent his campaign manager to appeal to Perot to drop out of the race and throw his support to Dole. Perot campaign aides rejected the plea and the outspoken Texan was expected to make his position clear in no uncertain terms.

"This was a terrible move, an act of desperation," American University political analyst Mark Rozell said. "It makes Dole look weak by going to Perot, whose support is also weak. Dole should have known better."

Rozell said presidential campaigns traditionally tighten in the final days. Four years ago, then-President George Bush cut Clinton's lead in half in the last two weeks, although he still lost by six points.

But Rozell said Dole's move made such tightening less likely to happen this year. "This admission of weakness could diminish Dole's prospects in the home stretch. It may demoralise Republican activists and potentially hurt the party all the way down the ticket."
This is important since Republicans are in a tough fight to cling to control of Congress, which they won two years ago.

Perot is still furious at Dole, whom he blames for insisting on his exclusion from the presidential debates. He is also contemptuous of Dole's 15 percent income tax cut proposal, which he says will lead to an explosion in the federal budget deficit.
Perot's campaign manager Russ Verney said Dole's appeal, coming at the 11th hour of the campaign and after he kept Perot out of the debates, was "absolutely foolish".

Even if Perot did agree to drop out, his standing in most recent polls was only between four and eight percent -- insufficient to close the gap with Clinton even if they all voted for Dole, which would not happen.
"If Perot did drop out, which he will not, it would only narrow the race nationally by two or three percentage points at most," Reuters pollster John Zogby said.

A shift of two or three points could be significant in states where the race is extremely tight like Florida, Alabama, North Carolina and Virginia. But these are all traditional Republican states that Dole should have locked up weeks ago and even if he won all of them Clinton would still easily win the election.

Euel Elliott, a political scientist at the University of Texas in Dallas, said with Perot viewed negatively by most of the electorate an endorsement from him would have limited value and might even be harmful.
"There's at least as much chance of this blowing up in Dole's face as doing some good," he said. "Perot's support would not necessarily mostly go to Dole in any case."

Georgetown University professor Steven Wayne said Dole had t managed to shake up the race for a day or two. "But the die has been cast for president. The only thing we don't know yet is how far Clinton's victory carries over to the congressional elections," he said.
